questions.q: Define “prudential reason” for power sharing in one sentence, using the exact terminology from the chapter.
questions.a: A prudential reason for power sharing is a practical, calculation-based justification that stresses how sharing power reduces conflict, ensures political stability, and prevents the tyranny of the majority. A wrong answer — such as “it is the morally right thing to do” — reveals the student is confusing prudential with moral reasoning, a frequent board-exam error that costs marks in distinction-type questions.

questions.q: Explain why the moral argument for power sharing cannot be reduced to merely “keeping the peace.”
questions.a: The moral argument holds that power sharing is a democratic right in itself: citizens have a stake in decisions affecting them, and excluding groups violates their dignity and autonomy, regardless of whether conflict erupts. A wrong answer that equates moral reasons with “avoiding violence” shows the student misses the normative core — that legitimacy comes from participation, not just order — a distinction CBSE often tests in “explain” questions.

questions.q: A new country’s constitution grants minority groups veto power over laws affecting their culture. The prime minister says, “We do this because otherwise the minorities will revolt.” Identify the type of reasoning used and justify your choice.
questions.a: The prime minister uses prudential reasoning: the justification is the practical fear of revolt (instability), not the inherent right of minorities to self-governance. A student who labels this “moral” because it “protects minorities” fails to see that the motive is consequence-driven, not principle-driven — a classic board-exam trap in case-based questions.

questions.q: Compare how the Belgian and Sri Lankan approaches reflect prudential versus moral reasoning. Which country’s model leans more on moral reasoning, and why?
questions.a: Belgium’s consociational model (equal representation, community vetoes) embodies moral reasoning by treating linguistic communities as equal partners with a right to co-govern. Sri Lanka’s majoritarian model (Sinhala Only Act, Buddhism foremost) ignored moral claims of Tamils, relying instead on a prudential gamble that majority dominance would unify the nation — which backfired. A wrong answer that says “both are prudential” misses the normative design of Belgium’s institutions, a key comparison point in CBSE long-answer questions.

questions.q: “Power sharing based only on prudential reasons is fragile.” Evaluate this statement with reference to the Sri Lankan experience.
questions.a: The statement is valid: Sri Lanka’s leaders initially adopted majoritarian policies believing they would strengthen national unity (a prudential calculation), but without moral inclusion, the Tamil minority felt permanently excluded, leading to civil war. Prudence without morality lacks legitimacy; when calculations change, the arrangement collapses. A student who argues “prudence alone works if the majority is benevolent” misunderstands that democratic stability requires institutionalized moral recognition, not contingent goodwill — a nuance CBSE expects in evaluation questions.

questions.q: Draft a two-paragraph speech for a Model UN delegate arguing that a proposed power-sharing pact for a fictional divided society must embed both prudential and moral clauses. Each paragraph must explicitly name one type of reason and give a concrete mechanism.
questions.a: Paragraph 1 (prudential): “We propose a rotating presidency and mutual veto on security laws because history shows that without such checks, one group’s dominance triggers rebellion — as in Sri Lanka.” Paragraph 2 (moral): “We also mandate proportional representation in the cabinet because every community’s right to govern itself is a democratic entitlement, not a concession — as Belgium’s community governments demonstrate.” A weak answer that mixes mechanisms without labeling the reasoning type shows the student cannot operationalize the distinction in policy design, a skill tested in CBSE competency-based case studies.

questions.q: Fill in the blank: ______ reasons for power sharing emphasize practical, calculated benefits such as political stability, conflict prevention, and the avoidance of majority tyranny, arguing that sharing power reduces the risk of social unrest and regime collapse.
Fill in the blank: Imagine your school’s student council is dominated by one ______ group that decides all events and rules without consulting others.
What must you be able to do to master this topic?
questions.a: The student can clearly distinguish prudential from moral justifications for power sharing, cite specific examples from the Belgium and Sri Lanka case studies to illustrate each type, and explain why a durable democracy requires both practical stability and ethical legitimacy.
